summary: Gives guidelines for using IPv6 transition mechanisms during IPv6 deployment, helping operators choose among the many deployment models. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Many ways exist to move to the new internet addresses. This is a guide for picking one.

questions: which ipv6 deployment model should i use
subtitle: Advice on which IPv6 deployment model to pick, from dual stack to IPv6-only with translation.

tldr.problem: Network managers face many IPv6 deployment models and tools, built over the years for different circumstances, and need guidance on which to use as IPv4 addresses run short.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out principles for choosing a model, then recommends four: native dual stack, tunneling across IPv4 islands, an IPv6-only core running Dual Stack Lite, and IPv6-only deployment with translation.
tldr.outcome: The fundamental recommendation is to turn on IPv6. The first two models are the most widely deployed and should take priority where they apply.

today: RFC 6180 is an Informational RFC (May 2011) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It reflects the situation at the time of writing, including the August 2010 IANA figures.

sections.title: Why a Transition Guide Is Needed
sections.content:
The text was written when the IANA free pool held only 14 unallocated unicast IPv4 /8 prefixes, and the Regional Internet Registries were expected to exhaust their space by early 2012. The RFC says IPv6 is the only real option for more address space.

IPv6 deployment takes effort, resources and expertise, and the many deployment models and tools developed at the IETF differ greatly in how they work. Network managers are confused, so the document recommends approaches for common situations. It does not cover every network, and each manager must choose the best solution for their own case.
sections.plainLanguage: The old street-number system is running out of numbers. People can switch to a new system in many ways, and this guide helps them choose.

sections.title: Principles for Choosing a Model
sections.content:
The end goal is network-wide native IPv6, which would make tunnels, encapsulation and translation obsolete, and IPv4 too. Transition mechanisms are a means to that end. The RFC says there is no point in waiting for an improved design, because the migration tools already exist.

When choosing, the model must let communication flow without perceived degradation. Ability to communicate matters more than fine-grained performance, so existing tools are often preferred over new ones, and tools that can be dropped after coexistence are preferred over ones that need permanent changes. Incremental deployability, simplicity, scalability and the ability to maintain and diagnose the network also count.

Deployment is normally step-wise. For example, IPv6 connectivity has to be established and tested before DNS entries with IPv6 addresses are provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the plan that works for everyone and is easy to undo later. Do not wait for a perfect plan, because the good ones already exist.

sections.title: The Four Recommended Models
sections.content:
Native dual stack (4.1) turns on IPv6 throughout the existing IPv4 network so both run side by side. It is the recommended model for most networks and avoids tunnel and MTU problems. Its challenges are that real use needs the peer to be reachable over IPv6 and listed in DNS, and that some applications switch slowly to IPv4 when IPv6 works unreliably. Some content providers and network managers have agreed to resolve names to IPv6 addresses only for each other, a practice the RFC calls whitelisting, which creates a dependency on an outside party.

Crossing IPv4 islands (4.2) uses tunnels when native IPv6 is not available. Tunneling adds complexity and more reliance on Path MTU, but it decouples addressing inside and outside the tunnel. On unmanaged networks, early-adopter solutions such as 6to4 have at times made IPv6 look available when it was not. 6rd (RFC 5969) is described as a newer version of 6to4 without those drawbacks.

IPv6-only core (4.3) uses IPv6 in a service provider network and tunnels IPv4 through it. The recommended tool is Dual Stack Lite.

IPv6-only deployment (4.4) fits when an IPv4-only domain and an IPv6-only domain must talk to each other. It can use proxies or relays at the application level, which the RFC prefers over application layer gateways in translators, or network-layer IPv4/IPv6 translation (RFC 6144).
sections.plainLanguage: There are four routes. Run both address systems side by side, build a tunnel across the old-only parts, run the middle of the network on the new system, or go all new and use a translator at the edges.

sections.title: Translation and Its Limits
sections.content:
Network-layer translation can offer two services to IPv6-only hosts. A small set of systems may be configured with IPv4-mapped addresses, giving stateless interoperation between the IPv4-only and IPv6-only domains. A larger set of systems with global IPv6 addresses can reach IPv4 servers through stateful translation, but cannot be reached as peers or servers from the IPv4-only domain. The stateless service suits servers and the stateful one suits large numbers of client devices.

The RFC names two challenges. While IPv4 addresses are still shared, issues similar to those of IPv4 NATs appear. And IPv4 literals in formats such as HTML fail on IPv6-only hosts, since the host has no IPv4 address or route. Proxies, host mapping of IPv4 literals to IPv6 addresses, or native dual stack are the suggested fixes.

The older NAT-PT design (RFC 2766) is described as problematic and was deprecated for the reasons in RFC 4966. The RFC also prefers tunneling over double translation when an IPv4 or IPv6 segment must be crossed.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator is like an interpreter between two people who speak different languages. It works well, but a few things, like a phone number written in the old style, get lost.

sections.title: Conclusions and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The fundamental recommendation is to turn on IPv6. All four models are recommended by the IETF, but the first two should take priority where they apply. The RFC admits the mechanisms operators deployed have been a mixed blessing: dual stack is underused if peers have not upgraded, tunnels that do not follow the underlying routing have been problematic, and translation has faults too. Still, operators have deployed very large networks with these models.

It lists considerations: there is a trade-off between connecting many device types and moving forward independently; new ("greenfield") networks differ from ones with existing IPv4 users; and the right choice changes over time. Whatever the model, IPv6 must also be handled in network management, address assignment, service agreements, firewalls and intrusion detection systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The big message is to get started. Any of the four routes beats waiting, and you can change routes later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPv4 and IPv6 provide a very similar level of security and face the same threats, with specific issues more likely found in practice, such as product bugs, than in the specifications. When deploying IPv6, the network components must have the necessary security capabilities for IPv6 traffic. Firewall capabilities have often been a challenge.

This document has no impact on the security of specific transition tools. Their own documents cover that, for example RFC 4213, RFC 6147 and RFC 6169.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system is about as safe as the old one. Just make sure your locks and alarms work with it too.
